**The empire in which Alexey Brodovitch was born was the Russian Empire.  
The events that dissolved its privileges were the February 1917 and October 1917 Revolutions, and the subsequent Soviet decrees that abolished the aristocracy and its legal privileges.**

---

| Event | What happened | Why it matters to Brodovitch’s “birth empire” |
|-------|---------------|----------------------------------------------|
| **February Revolution (21 March 1917, Julian calendar)** | The Tsar and the autocratic monarchy were overthrown. A provisional government took power. | It formally ended the uninterrupted rule of the Romanov dynasty, the same system that had granted hereditary privileges to families such as the Brodovitchs. |
| **October (November) Revolution (6 November 1917)** | The Bolsheviks seized power, dissolved the Provisional Government and established a Soviet state. | The new Soviet regime actively outlawed the very privileges (titles, lands, soldier‑status, etc.) that the Romanovs had enjoyed. |
| **Decree of the Council of People's Commissars (12 January 1918)** | A decree that abolished the privileges of the nobility, confiscated their lands, and declared all Russian citizens equal before the law. | This was the legal instrument that struck the last formal stamp out of the “privileges” of the Russian birth‑empire. |
| **Treaty of Brest‑Litovsk (March 1918)** | Russia ceded vast territories to the Central Powers and effectively ended Russia’s participation in WWI. | It was the final blow that shattered the political‑territorial structure of the empire, proving its dissolution. |
| **1924 Constitution of the USSR** | Formal constitution of the Soviet Union, which continued the abolition of aristocratic privileges. | While the Russian Empire no longer existed, the legal framework that had protected Brodovitch’s family’s birth‑status had already been eliminated. |

---

### Bottom line

The privileges tied to the Russian Empire – noble titles, land ownership, preferential status in the army and civil service, and the hereditary dignity that families like the Brodovitchs enjoyed – were officially ended by:

1. The overthrow of the Romanov monarchy in 1917, and  
2. The Soviet decrees that abolished aristocratic rights and privileges in 1918 (and were cemented in subsequent Soviet law).

Thus, the **Bolshevik Revolution of 1917** (and its legal aftermath) dissolved the privileges of Alexey Brodovitch’s birth empire.

**Alexey Vyacheslavovich Brodovitch** (also **Brodovich**; Belarusian: Аляксей Брадовіч, Russian: Алексе́й Вячесла́вович Бродо́вич; 1898–April 15, 1971) was a Russian-American photographer, art director, and educator of Belarusian descent. He is most famous for his work as art director of American fashion magazine _[Harper's Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's\_Bazaar "Harper's Bazaar")_ from 1934 to 1958.

## Early life in Russia
[edit]
Alexey Brodovitch was born in Ogolichi[ru], Russian Empire (now Belarus) to a wealthy family in 1898. His father, Cheslau or Vyacheslav Brodovitch, was a respected physician, psychiatrist and huntsman. His mother was an amateur painter. During the Russo-Japanese War, his family moved to Moscow, where his father worked in a hospital for Japanese prisoners. Alexey was sent to study at the Prince Tenisheff School, a prestigious institution in Saint Petersburg, with the intentions of eventually enrolling in the Imperial Art Academy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-p12-1) He had no formal training in art through his childhood, but often sketched noble profiles in the audience at concerts in the city.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-B72-40-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-Brodovitch,_Alexey_p3-3)
Brodovitch in Russia
At the start of World War I at the young age of 16, Brodovitch abandoned his dream of entering the Imperial Art Academy and ran away from home to join the Russian army. Not long after, his father had him brought home and hired a private tutor to help Alexey finish school. Upon graduating, Brodovitch ran away again on several occasions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-p12-1) He recalls:
> After a week or so I ran away to the front line to kill Germans. But my father, now a military general at the head of a Red Cross hospital train, had plenty of influence, and I was soon brought back to him. On the train back I was employed as a nurses' aid. In East Prussia I ran away again and joined a nearby regiment. Once again I was caught, and this time I was sent to an officers' school, the Corps de Pages.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-4)

## Early life in Russia
During the Russian Civil War, Brodovitch served with the White Army. While fighting against the Bolsheviks in Odessa, he was badly wounded and was hospitalized for a time in Kislovodsk, in the Caucasus. In 1918, the town was surrounded by the Bolsheviks, forcing Brodovitch into exile. It was during this retreat to the south through Caucasus and Turkey that he met his future wife, Nina.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-B72-40-2)
By good fortune, Alexey's brother Nicolas turned out to be one of the soldiers guarding the refugees in Novorossiysk. Not long after, their father, who had been imprisoned in Saint Petersburg by the Bolsheviks, managed to flee to Novorossiysk in hopes of finding his family. The three were once again together, and arranged for Brodovitch's mother and other relations to join them in Constantinople. Finally reunited, the Brodovitchs made their way to France.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-5)

## Influential years in Paris
[edit]
Upon arriving in Paris, Brodovitch wanted to be a painter. A Russian white émigré in Paris, Brodovitch found himself poor and having to work for the first time in his life. He took a job painting houses, while his wife Nina worked as a seamstress.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-6) They lived in a cheap, small apartment in the area of Montparnasse, among Russian artists who had settled in Paris at the end of the 19th century. This group of artists, including Archipenko, Chagall, and Nathan Altman, would meet at the inexpensive Académie Vassilieff, which offered painting and sculpting classes without an instructor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-7) His connections with these young Russian artists led to more artistic work as a painter of backdrops for Diaghilev's _Ballets Russes._[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-8)
Paris was a cosmopolitan city through which many artists and art movements passed. Brodovitch was exposed to everything from Dadaism from Zurich and Berlin, Suprematism and Constructivism from Moscow, Bauhaus design from Germany, Futurism from Italy, De Stijl from the Netherlands, and the native strains of Cubism, Fauvism, Purism and Surrealism. Among these various artistic influences, Brodovitch found his beginnings as a designer.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-9)

## Influential years in Paris
### Move to graphic arts
[edit]
On nights and weekends away from the _Ballets Russes_, Brodovitch began sketching designs for textiles, china, and jewelry. By the time his work for the ballet had finished, he had already compiled an extensive portfolio of these side projects and was selling his designs to fashionable shops.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-10) He worked part-time doing layouts for _[Cahiers d'Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahiers\_d'Art "Cahiers d'Art")_, an important art journal, and _Arts et Métiers Graphiques_, an influential design magazine. While working on layouts, Brodovitch was responsible for fitting together type, photographs, and illustrations on the pages of the magazines. He had the rare opportunity of having influence over the look of the magazine as there was no art director.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-11)

## Biography
Alexey Vyacheslavovich Brodovitch was born in 1898 in Ogolichi, then part of the Russian Empire. He served in the Imperial Russian Army during the First World War and the subsequent civil war, fought on the White side, and eventually made his way out of Russia via Constantinople to Paris.
In Paris through the 1920s he moved through the graphic arts — painting sets for the Ballets Russes, designing posters, and winning a poster competition for the Bal Banal in 1924 in which Picasso also entered. He ran the studio at the Parisian department store Trois Quartiers and absorbed the European avant-garde around him — Cassandre’s posters, the Bauhaus émigrés, the Constructivists he already knew from home.
In 1930 he moved to Philadelphia to run the advertising-design programme at the Pennsylvania Museum School of Industrial Art. In 1934 Carmel Snow hired him as art director of _Harper’s Bazaar_. He held the post until 1958 — twenty-four years that remade American magazine design.
From 1941 he ran the Design Laboratory, first at the New School for Social Research and then independently. It was never a conventional course. Students brought work; Brodovitch tore it up. Those who survived included Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Diane Arbus, Hiro and Art Kane.
His later years were difficult. Ill health, alcoholism and two studio fires that destroyed most of his personal archive pushed him into retreat. He returned to France in the mid-1960s and died in Le Thor in 1971, largely in obscurity.
02

## Design philosophy
Brodovitch’s position was that the editorial spread — not the single page — is the unit of design, and that typography and photography have to be composed as a single image.
> “Astonish me!” — Alexey Brodovitch, to students and contributors
The two-word brief became legendary because it was genuine. He refused to tell photographers what he wanted. He expected them to bring him something he hadn’t seen before, and he edited ruthlessly when they didn’t.
His working principle was that **white space is the designer’s best friend**. A Brodovitch spread is never full. Type sits against deliberately empty paper. An image bleeds across the gutter so that the fold itself becomes part of the composition. Type is treated photographically — its weight and placement answering the weight and placement of the image across the spread.
He was not a theorist. He left no textbook, no manifesto, almost no writing. What he left was the practice and the students who carried it.
03

## Key works
**Harper’s Bazaar art direction (1934–1958)** — the role that built the reputation. Twenty-four years of monthly issues under Carmel Snow, with Brodovitch commissioning and editing Cartier-Bresson, Man Ray, Bill Brandt, Avedon, Penn and dozens more. The integrated spread — photograph, headline and body treated as one composition — is his permanent contribution to editorial craft.
**Ballet (1945)** — Brodovitch’s own photo book, printed in photogravure in a small edition by J. J. Augustin. Motion-blurred, grainy, deliberately imperfect images of the Ballets Russes taken from the wings during the 1930s. Ignored on publication, now recognised as one of the foundational photo books of the century.
**Portfolio magazine (1949–1951)** — three issues only, co-founded with Frank Zachary. Large format, no advertising, high-quality printing with fold-outs, die-cuts and tipped-in materials. The magazine went bankrupt but every subsequent art-publication designer has studied it.
**Observations (1959)** — book with photographs by Richard Avedon and text by Truman Capote, designed by Brodovitch. The spread discipline from _Bazaar_ applied to the book page — images scaled, cropped and paired against type with complete confidence.
**The Design Laboratory (1941–1967)** — not a physical artefact but a teaching programme. The list of its students is effectively a list of mid-century American photography and design. It may be the longest-lasting work he did.
**WWII Four Freedoms posters (1942)** — a series of Spanish-language propaganda posters for the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. Distributed across Latin America, they show the same cropped-figure composition against open space that Brodovitch used in the magazine context, transferred to the poster format without modification.
**New Poster exhibition catalogue (1937)** — catalogue design for the International Exposition of Design in Outdoor Advertising at the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia. The cover, held at the Library of Congress, shows Brodovitch operating simultaneously as magazine art director, design educator and exhibition designer.

## Key works
### Harper's Bazaar art direction
1934/1958
Twenty-four years as art director of Harper's Bazaar under editor Carmel Snow, from 1934 to 1958. Brodovitch commissioned work from Henri Cartier-Bresson, Man Ray, Bill Brandt, Richard Avedon and Irving Penn, treating each spread as a single composed image rather than a container for separate elements. Issues from this period are held in research collections at institutions including MoMA and the Cooper Hewitt Smithsonian Design Museum in New York.
Harper's Bazaar art direction (1934/1958). · People's Graphic Design Archive, item 4561. Statutory educational licence. · AU statutory

## Key works
### Ballet
1945
Brodovitch's own photo essay on ballet rehearsals, shot during the 1930s tours of the Ballets Russes de Monte Carlo using a Contax 35mm camera without flash. Published in 1945 by J. J. Augustin in New York in a small edition using photogravure printing; controversial on publication for its motion blur and grain. A facsimile edition was published by Errata Editions in 2011; original copies are held at MoMA and the Art Institute of Chicago.
Ballet (1945). · Little Steidl, 2024 facsimile of 1945 J. J. Augustin original. Statutory educational licence. · AU statutory

## Key works
### Portfolio magazine
1949/1951
Three issues only, co-founded with Frank Zachary and published by Zebra Press. A large-format journal of the graphic arts, printed with fold-outs, die-cuts and tipped-in materials and carrying no advertising. Production costs closed the magazine after three issues, but its design has been studied by subsequent art-publication designers and editors.
Portfolio magazine (1949/1951). · Ikonographia reproduction of Issue 1 spread, pages 2–3. Statutory educational licence. · AU statutory

## Key works
### Observations
1959
Designed by Brodovitch with photographs by Richard Avedon and text by Truman Capote, published by Simon and Schuster in New York in 1959. Avedon's photographs are portraits of public figures from the arts, politics and entertainment; Brodovitch's layouts used bleed images, asymmetric cropping and deliberate white space, applying the spread discipline from Harper's Bazaar directly to the book page. MoMA and the Art Institute of Chicago hold copies.
Observations (1959). · Victoria and Albert Museum, object O1744184. Public domain. · Public domain

## Key works
### Design Laboratory teaching programme
1941/1967
The teaching workshop Brodovitch ran from 1941, first at the New School for Social Research in New York and later as an independent programme. Students brought existing work for intensive critique rather than instruction in technique; Brodovitch's method was to demand work he had not seen before. Alumni include Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Diane Arbus, Hiro and Art Kane.
Design Laboratory teaching programme (1941/1967). · Modernism101. Statutory educational licence. · AU statutory

## Key works
### "Libertad de Palabra" — WWII poster
1942
One of a series of Spanish-language propaganda posters Brodovitch designed for the US war effort in 1942, adapted from Franklin D. Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech of January 1941. The posters were distributed across Latin America by the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. The series shows Brodovitch working outside the editorial context — a figure cropped tight against negative space, type subordinated to image, the photographic instinct of the magazine work applied directly to the poster format.
"Libertad de Palabra" (Freedom of Speech), 1942. Spanish-language WWII poster. · Illinois State University / Digital Public Library of America via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain. · Public domain

## First Draft
9 min read
Feb 16, 2016

Born in Ogolitchi, Russia, in 1898, Alexey Brodovitch was born into a wealthy aristocratic family. His father was a military physician and his mother was an amateur painter. Growing up, Brodovitch spent a lot of time taking photos with a box camera at his dad’s hospital, and this cultivated his interest in the military and photography. In 1914, he enrolled in a progressive school in St.Petersburg, and when it was time for him to graduate, he wanted to fight for the czar’s army instead of graduating. In 1918 he served in the white army of the czar, and during the war he temporarily paralyzed his right side. He was treated in a hospital where he met his wife, Nina. Nina and Brodovitch eloped to Paris in 1920, where Brodovitch started a career designing sets for Ballet Russe. He was very interested in the integration of dance, music, and scene design. Despite designing during a time where Art Deco was the most prominent movement, Brodovitch grew a natural antipathy towards the ornamental. Brodovitch was also designing porcelain, glass, and textiles for artists and designers like Piret, Rodier, and Bianchini, and making layouts for Cahiers d’Art and Arts et Metiers Graphiques. His career in Graphic Design formally launched when he won the Bal Banal Poster competition over prominent artists of the time, including Pablo Picasso. Between 1915 to 1930, he started to specialize in poster design. In 1930, he was approached by John Story Jenks to create a program for Advertising Design in the Philadelphia Muesum School of Art.

## First Draft
Brodovitch quickly became adapted to life in the United States, and he went on to be involved in projects like designing for ad agencies, starting design laboratories, being an instructor of design, and eventually a visiting critic. Carmel Snow, the new editor of Harper’s Bazaar at the time, noticed his work in his exhibitions for the Artist Directors Club and recruited him to create content for Junior Bazaar, a section in the back of Harper’s Bazaar. Staffed with Richard Avedon and Bob Cato, he was given free rein to do as he wished, and what started out as a section in the Harper’s Bazaar became its own booklet. He then became the art director of Harper’s Bazaar, a job he is now known for. He used the magazine to showcase young art, design, and photographic talent. He developed a style of using contrast and typography as the most important visual tools, and he used white space and bleeds extensively to emphasize certain movements and structures in photographs. While at Harper’s Bazaar, he held different roles in different disciplines of design, dabbling in industrial design and holding jobs as art directors at Saks Fifth Avenue and I. Miller. In 1950, he designed and cultivated a short-lived graphic design magazine that became a culmination of design ideas in the 1920’s and 1930’s. It was considered the most well-designed magazine to date, and it introduced talents through all disciplines in the arts. Soon after the magazine failed to be a long-term endeavour due to how expensive it was to produce, he moved back to France and eventually dies in Le Thor in 1971.

## First Draft
### Second Draft
Throughout the fifty years of Alexey Brodovitch’s working life, he has never stopped pushing the boundaries and culture of design as a job and discipline. He practiced design using the words of poet Ezra Pound as philosophy: “make it new.” He has held jobs in all realms of Art and Design, from painting sets for the Ballet Russe in Paris to tackling knock-down furniture design in his late 40’s, but he has never developed a specific style or codified set of rules in his work, as he believed in dynamism and progression through media.
Brodovitch was born in 1898 into a wealthy aristocratic family in Ogolitchi, Russia. His father was a military physician, and during the Russo-Japanese War that broke out in 1905, Brodovitch’s father was assigned to a hospital in Moscow to tend to soldiers in the frontier. Brodovitch often visited his father at the hospital with his box camera and took photos of Japanese prisoners of war. Taking photos at the hospital sparked his interest in photography while developing his yearn to be a part of the army. Because Brodovitch grew up amidst the turnover of tradition and conservation and the introduction of radically new and modern values, he grew to be hyperaware of the new and the different.

## First Draft
### Second Draft
After the Russo-Japanese War, Brodovitch’s family moved back to St. Petersburg, where Brodovitch attended Prince Tenisheff school, one of the most progressive schools in St. Petersburg. Living in St. Petersburg during this time played a major role in developing Brodovitch’s outlook on modernism. St. Petersburg had become a hub for Russia’s forced modernization, and with the influx of people and industries, St. Petersburg became a breeding ground for creativity and imagination for young minds like Brodovitch. When it came time for Brodovitch to graduate from Prince Tenisheff school, World War I broke out. With the outbreak of the war, St. Petersburg became infused with the spirit of patriotism and war, and Brodovitch was intoxicated. Batting away the sounds of protest from his parents and their attempts to pull him out of the military, Brodovitch eventually became enrolled in the Corps des Pages, an officers’ school, and eight months after the war had started he became the observant lieutenant of the white army of the Czar. His time fighting in the war ultimately made him a refugee of the war, as he was forced into exile while being hospitalized in Kislovodsk, a city that was captured by the Bolsheviks in 1918. During his escape from Kislovodsk, he met his wife Nina, and together they fled to Paris, the only place in 1920 that accepted the artistic and political revolution that was ongoing in Europe.
Being a white émigré, Brodovitch was stripped of his wealth and aristocracy and forced to find any work he could. His identity as an émigré made him feel alone and rejected, a feeling that he couldn’t escape even at the end of his life. Many attribute his aloofness to his inability to shake his identity as an émigré, and his use of white space in his work can be seen as a metaphor for his longing for the white plains of his homeland, Russia.

## First Draft
### Second Draft
While in Paris he struggled to find work, and he took up whatever job he could find. He reluctantly became a house painter while Nina became a seamstress. Through his frequenting the Académie Vassilieff, founded by Marie Vassilieff and used as a meeting ground for Russian émigrés and French artists, Brodovitch was introduced to the avant-garde artistic scene of Paris. Through these connections he got the job of being a backdrop painter for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russe. It was the Ballet Russe that cultivated Brodovitch’s strong belief in the integration of different disciplines into one coherent production, a belief that later played a big role in his development as an art director at Harper’s Bazaar. Brodovitch did not settle for a job working on the sets of Ballet Russe. He was relentless in his efforts to find more work, so he could provide a better life for him and his family. While still working on the Ballet Russe, he designed porcelain, glass, and textiles for famous designers such as Piret, Rodier, and Bianchini. He also made layouts for Cahiers d’Art and Arts et Metiers Graphiques, and he quickly made a name for himself. Because of his active role in several realms of art and design, he was particularly astute to visual trends. In 1924, he was invited to design a poster for the Bal Banal, a party organized to help compatriots. His poster was chosen over the likes of Pablo Picasso and other prominent artists at the time, and this was the first work of his that was widely received by the artistic community and it became the impetus to his career as a graphic designer. Under the influence of visual trends, he combined the decorum of Art Deco, the geometry of Purism, and the discontinuous imagery of Surrealism into his works.

## First Draft

Born in Ogolitchi, Russia, in 1898, Alexey Brodovitch was born into a wealthy aristocratic family. His father was a military physician and his mother was an amateur painter. Growing up, Brodovitch spent a lot of time taking photos with a box camera at his dad’s hospital, and this cultivated his interest in the military and photography. In 1914, he enrolled in a progressive school in St.Petersburg, and when it was time for him to graduate, he wanted to fight for the czar’s army instead of graduating. In 1918 he served in the white army of the czar, and during the war he temporarily paralyzed his right side. He was treated in a hospital where he met his wife, Nina. Nina and Brodovitch eloped to Paris in 1920, where Brodovitch started a career designing sets for Ballet Russe. He was very interested in the integration of dance, music, and scene design. Despite designing during a time where Art Deco was the most prominent movement, Brodovitch grew a natural antipathy towards the ornamental. Brodovitch was also designing porcelain, glass, and textiles for artists and designers like Piret, Rodier, and Bianchini, and making layouts for Cahiers d’Art and Arts et Metiers Graphiques. His career in Graphic Design formally launched when he won the Bal Banal Poster competition over prominent artists of the time, including Pablo Picasso. Between 1915 to 1930, he started to specialize in poster design. In 1930, he was approached by John Story Jenks to create a program for Advertising Design in the Philadelphia Muesum School of Art.

## First Draft
Brodovitch quickly became adapted to life in the United States, and he went on to be involved in projects like designing for ad agencies, starting design laboratories, being an instructor of design, and eventually a visiting critic. Carmel Snow, the new editor of Harper’s Bazaar at the time, noticed his work in his exhibitions for the Artist Directors Club and recruited him to create content for Junior Bazaar, a section in the back of Harper’s Bazaar. Staffed with Richard Avedon and Bob Cato, he was given free rein to do as he wished, and what started out as a section in the Harper’s Bazaar became its own booklet. He then became the art director of Harper’s Bazaar, a job he is now known for. He used the magazine to showcase young art, design, and photographic talent. He developed a style of using contrast and typography as the most important visual tools, and he used white space and bleeds extensively to emphasize certain movements and structures in photographs. While at Harper’s Bazaar, he held different roles in different disciplines of design, dabbling in industrial design and holding jobs as art directors at Saks Fifth Avenue and I. Miller. In 1950, he designed and cultivated a short-lived graphic design magazine that became a culmination of design ideas in the 1920’s and 1930’s. It was considered the most well-designed magazine to date, and it introduced talents through all disciplines in the arts. Soon after the magazine failed to be a long-term endeavour due to how expensive it was to produce, he moved back to France and eventually dies in Le Thor in 1971.

## First Draft
### Second Draft
Throughout the fifty years of Alexey Brodovitch’s working life, he has never stopped pushing the boundaries and culture of design as a job and discipline. He practiced design using the words of poet Ezra Pound as philosophy: “make it new.” He has held jobs in all realms of Art and Design, from painting sets for the Ballet Russe in Paris to tackling knock-down furniture design in his late 40’s, but he has never developed a specific style or codified set of rules in his work, as he believed in dynamism and progression through media.
Brodovitch was born in 1898 into a wealthy aristocratic family in Ogolitchi, Russia. His father was a military physician, and during the Russo-Japanese War that broke out in 1905, Brodovitch’s father was assigned to a hospital in Moscow to tend to soldiers in the frontier. Brodovitch often visited his father at the hospital with his box camera and took photos of Japanese prisoners of war. Taking photos at the hospital sparked his interest in photography while developing his yearn to be a part of the army. Because Brodovitch grew up amidst the turnover of tradition and conservation and the introduction of radically new and modern values, he grew to be hyperaware of the new and the different.

## First Draft
### Second Draft
After the Russo-Japanese War, Brodovitch’s family moved back to St. Petersburg, where Brodovitch attended Prince Tenisheff school, one of the most progressive schools in St. Petersburg. Living in St. Petersburg during this time played a major role in developing Brodovitch’s outlook on modernism. St. Petersburg had become a hub for Russia’s forced modernization, and with the influx of people and industries, St. Petersburg became a breeding ground for creativity and imagination for young minds like Brodovitch. When it came time for Brodovitch to graduate from Prince Tenisheff school, World War I broke out. With the outbreak of the war, St. Petersburg became infused with the spirit of patriotism and war, and Brodovitch was intoxicated. Batting away the sounds of protest from his parents and their attempts to pull him out of the military, Brodovitch eventually became enrolled in the Corps des Pages, an officers’ school, and eight months after the war had started he became the observant lieutenant of the white army of the Czar. His time fighting in the war ultimately made him a refugee of the war, as he was forced into exile while being hospitalized in Kislovodsk, a city that was captured by the Bolsheviks in 1918. During his escape from Kislovodsk, he met his wife Nina, and together they fled to Paris, the only place in 1920 that accepted the artistic and political revolution that was ongoing in Europe.
Being a white émigré, Brodovitch was stripped of his wealth and aristocracy and forced to find any work he could. His identity as an émigré made him feel alone and rejected, a feeling that he couldn’t escape even at the end of his life. Many attribute his aloofness to his inability to shake his identity as an émigré, and his use of white space in his work can be seen as a metaphor for his longing for the white plains of his homeland, Russia.

## First Draft
### Second Draft
While in Paris he struggled to find work, and he took up whatever job he could find. He reluctantly became a house painter while Nina became a seamstress. Through his frequenting the Académie Vassilieff, founded by Marie Vassilieff and used as a meeting ground for Russian émigrés and French artists, Brodovitch was introduced to the avant-garde artistic scene of Paris. Through these connections he got the job of being a backdrop painter for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russe. It was the Ballet Russe that cultivated Brodovitch’s strong belief in the integration of different disciplines into one coherent production, a belief that later played a big role in his development as an art director at Harper’s Bazaar. Brodovitch did not settle for a job working on the sets of Ballet Russe. He was relentless in his efforts to find more work, so he could provide a better life for him and his family. While still working on the Ballet Russe, he designed porcelain, glass, and textiles for famous designers such as Piret, Rodier, and Bianchini. He also made layouts for Cahiers d’Art and Arts et Metiers Graphiques, and he quickly made a name for himself. Because of his active role in several realms of art and design, he was particularly astute to visual trends. In 1924, he was invited to design a poster for the Bal Banal, a party organized to help compatriots. His poster was chosen over the likes of Pablo Picasso and other prominent artists at the time, and this was the first work of his that was widely received by the artistic community and it became the impetus to his career as a graphic designer. Under the influence of visual trends, he combined the decorum of Art Deco, the geometry of Purism, and the discontinuous imagery of Surrealism into his works.

**Alexey Vyacheslavovich Brodovitch** (also **Brodovich**; Belarusian: Аляксей Брадовіч, Russian: Алексе́й Вячесла́вович Бродо́вич; 1898–April 15, 1971) was a Russian-American photographer, art director, and educator of Belarusian descent. He is most famous for his work as art director of American fashion magazine _[Harper's Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper's\_Bazaar "Harper's Bazaar")_ from 1934 to 1958.
texts.1:
## Early life in Russia
[edit]
Alexey Brodovitch was born in Ogolichi[ru], Russian Empire (now Belarus) to a wealthy family in 1898. His father, Cheslau or Vyacheslav Brodovitch, was a respected physician, psychiatrist and huntsman. His mother was an amateur painter. During the Russo-Japanese War, his family moved to Moscow, where his father worked in a hospital for Japanese prisoners. Alexey was sent to study at the Prince Tenisheff School, a prestigious institution in Saint Petersburg, with the intentions of eventually enrolling in the Imperial Art Academy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-p12-1) He had no formal training in art through his childhood, but often sketched noble profiles in the audience at concerts in the city.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-B72-40-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-Brodovitch,_Alexey_p3-3)
Brodovitch in Russia
At the start of World War I at the young age of 16, Brodovitch abandoned his dream of entering the Imperial Art Academy and ran away from home to join the Russian army. Not long after, his father had him brought home and hired a private tutor to help Alexey finish school. Upon graduating, Brodovitch ran away again on several occasions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-p12-1) He recalls:
> After a week or so I ran away to the front line to kill Germans. But my father, now a military general at the head of a Red Cross hospital train, had plenty of influence, and I was soon brought back to him. On the train back I was employed as a nurses' aid. In East Prussia I ran away again and joined a nearby regiment. Once again I was caught, and this time I was sent to an officers' school, the Corps de Pages.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-4)

## Early life in Russia
During the Russian Civil War, Brodovitch served with the White Army. While fighting against the Bolsheviks in Odessa, he was badly wounded and was hospitalized for a time in Kislovodsk, in the Caucasus. In 1918, the town was surrounded by the Bolsheviks, forcing Brodovitch into exile. It was during this retreat to the south through Caucasus and Turkey that he met his future wife, Nina.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-B72-40-2)
By good fortune, Alexey's brother Nicolas turned out to be one of the soldiers guarding the refugees in Novorossiysk. Not long after, their father, who had been imprisoned in Saint Petersburg by the Bolsheviks, managed to flee to Novorossiysk in hopes of finding his family. The three were once again together, and arranged for Brodovitch's mother and other relations to join them in Constantinople. Finally reunited, the Brodovitchs made their way to France.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-5)
texts.3:
## Influential years in Paris
[edit]
Upon arriving in Paris, Brodovitch wanted to be a painter. A Russian white émigré in Paris, Brodovitch found himself poor and having to work for the first time in his life. He took a job painting houses, while his wife Nina worked as a seamstress.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-6) They lived in a cheap, small apartment in the area of Montparnasse, among Russian artists who had settled in Paris at the end of the 19th century. This group of artists, including Archipenko, Chagall, and Nathan Altman, would meet at the inexpensive Académie Vassilieff, which offered painting and sculpting classes without an instructor.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-7) His connections with these young Russian artists led to more artistic work as a painter of backdrops for Diaghilev's _Ballets Russes._[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-8)
Paris was a cosmopolitan city through which many artists and art movements passed. Brodovitch was exposed to everything from Dadaism from Zurich and Berlin, Suprematism and Constructivism from Moscow, Bauhaus design from Germany, Futurism from Italy, De Stijl from the Netherlands, and the native strains of Cubism, Fauvism, Purism and Surrealism. Among these various artistic influences, Brodovitch found his beginnings as a designer.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-9)

## Influential years in Paris
### Move to graphic arts
[edit]
On nights and weekends away from the _Ballets Russes_, Brodovitch began sketching designs for textiles, china, and jewelry. By the time his work for the ballet had finished, he had already compiled an extensive portfolio of these side projects and was selling his designs to fashionable shops.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-10) He worked part-time doing layouts for _[Cahiers d'Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahiers\_d'Art "Cahiers d'Art")_, an important art journal, and _Arts et Métiers Graphiques_, an influential design magazine. While working on layouts, Brodovitch was responsible for fitting together type, photographs, and illustrations on the pages of the magazines. He had the rare opportunity of having influence over the look of the magazine as there was no art director.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-11)

## Biography
Alexey Vyacheslavovich Brodovitch was born in 1898 in Ogolichi, then part of the Russian Empire. He served in the Imperial Russian Army during the First World War and the subsequent civil war, fought on the White side, and eventually made his way out of Russia via Constantinople to Paris.
In Paris through the 1920s he moved through the graphic arts — painting sets for the Ballets Russes, designing posters, and winning a poster competition for the Bal Banal in 1924 in which Picasso also entered. He ran the studio at the Parisian department store Trois Quartiers and absorbed the European avant-garde around him — Cassandre’s posters, the Bauhaus émigrés, the Constructivists he already knew from home.
In 1930 he moved to Philadelphia to run the advertising-design programme at the Pennsylvania Museum School of Industrial Art. In 1934 Carmel Snow hired him as art director of _Harper’s Bazaar_. He held the post until 1958 — twenty-four years that remade American magazine design.
From 1941 he ran the Design Laboratory, first at the New School for Social Research and then independently. It was never a conventional course. Students brought work; Brodovitch tore it up. Those who survived included Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Diane Arbus, Hiro and Art Kane.
His later years were difficult. Ill health, alcoholism and two studio fires that destroyed most of his personal archive pushed him into retreat. He returned to France in the mid-1960s and died in Le Thor in 1971, largely in obscurity.

## Design philosophy
Brodovitch’s position was that the editorial spread — not the single page — is the unit of design, and that typography and photography have to be composed as a single image.
> “Astonish me!” — Alexey Brodovitch, to students and contributors
The two-word brief became legendary because it was genuine. He refused to tell photographers what he wanted. He expected them to bring him something he hadn’t seen before, and he edited ruthlessly when they didn’t.
His working principle was that **white space is the designer’s best friend**. A Brodovitch spread is never full. Type sits against deliberately empty paper. An image bleeds across the gutter so that the fold itself becomes part of the composition. Type is treated photographically — its weight and placement answering the weight and placement of the image across the spread.
He was not a theorist. He left no textbook, no manifesto, almost no writing. What he left was the practice and the students who carried it.

## Key works
**Harper’s Bazaar art direction (1934–1958)** — the role that built the reputation. Twenty-four years of monthly issues under Carmel Snow, with Brodovitch commissioning and editing Cartier-Bresson, Man Ray, Bill Brandt, Avedon, Penn and dozens more. The integrated spread — photograph, headline and body treated as one composition — is his permanent contribution to editorial craft.
**Ballet (1945)** — Brodovitch’s own photo book, printed in photogravure in a small edition by J. J. Augustin. Motion-blurred, grainy, deliberately imperfect images of the Ballets Russes taken from the wings during the 1930s. Ignored on publication, now recognised as one of the foundational photo books of the century.
**Portfolio magazine (1949–1951)** — three issues only, co-founded with Frank Zachary. Large format, no advertising, high-quality printing with fold-outs, die-cuts and tipped-in materials. The magazine went bankrupt but every subsequent art-publication designer has studied it.
**Observations (1959)** — book with photographs by Richard Avedon and text by Truman Capote, designed by Brodovitch. The spread discipline from _Bazaar_ applied to the book page — images scaled, cropped and paired against type with complete confidence.
**The Design Laboratory (1941–1967)** — not a physical artefact but a teaching programme. The list of its students is effectively a list of mid-century American photography and design. It may be the longest-lasting work he did.
**WWII Four Freedoms posters (1942)** — a series of Spanish-language propaganda posters for the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. Distributed across Latin America, they show the same cropped-figure composition against open space that Brodovitch used in the magazine context, transferred to the poster format without modification.
**New Poster exhibition catalogue (1937)** — catalogue design for the International Exposition of Design in Outdoor Advertising at the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia. The cover, held at the Library of Congress, shows Brodovitch operating simultaneously as magazine art director, design educator and exhibition designer.

## Key works
### Harper's Bazaar art direction
1934/1958
Twenty-four years as art director of Harper's Bazaar under editor Carmel Snow, from 1934 to 1958. Brodovitch commissioned work from Henri Cartier-Bresson, Man Ray, Bill Brandt, Richard Avedon and Irving Penn, treating each spread as a single composed image rather than a container for separate elements. Issues from this period are held in research collections at institutions including MoMA and the Cooper Hewitt Smithsonian Design Museum in New York.

## Key works
### Ballet
1945
Brodovitch's own photo essay on ballet rehearsals, shot during the 1930s tours of the Ballets Russes de Monte Carlo using a Contax 35mm camera without flash. Published in 1945 by J. J. ### Portfolio magazine
1949/1951
Three issues only, co-founded with Frank Zachary and published by Zebra Press. A large-format journal of the graphic arts, printed with fold-outs, die-cuts and tipped-in materials and carrying no advertising. Production costs closed the magazine after three issues, but its design has been studied by subsequent art-publication designers and editors.

## Key works
### Observations
1959
Designed by Brodovitch with photographs by Richard Avedon and text by Truman Capote, published by Simon and Schuster in New York in 1959. Avedon's photographs are portraits of public figures from the arts, politics and entertainment; Brodovitch's layouts used bleed images, asymmetric cropping and deliberate white space, applying the spread discipline from Harper's Bazaar directly to the book page. MoMA and the Art Institute of Chicago hold copies.

## Key works
### Design Laboratory teaching programme
1941/1967
The teaching workshop Brodovitch ran from 1941, first at the New School for Social Research in New York and later as an independent programme. Students brought existing work for intensive critique rather than instruction in technique; Brodovitch's method was to demand work he had not seen before. Alumni include Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Diane Arbus, Hiro and Art Kane.

## Key works
### "Libertad de Palabra" — WWII poster
1942
One of a series of Spanish-language propaganda posters Brodovitch designed for the US war effort in 1942, adapted from Franklin D. Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech of January 1941. The posters were distributed across Latin America by the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. The series shows Brodovitch working outside the editorial context — a figure cropped tight against negative space, type subordinated to image, the photographic instinct of the magazine work applied directly to the poster format.

Alexey Brodovitch was born in Ogolichi[ru], Russian Empire (now Belarus) to a wealthy family in 1898. His father, Cheslau or Vyacheslav Brodovitch, was a respected physician, psychiatrist and huntsman. His mother was an amateur painter. During the Russo-Japanese War, his family moved to Moscow, where his father worked in a hospital for Japanese prisoners. Alexey was sent to study at the Prince Tenisheff School, a prestigious institution in Saint Petersburg, with the intentions of eventually enrolling in the Imperial Art Academy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-p12-1) He had no formal training in art through his childhood, but often sketched noble profiles in the audience at concerts in the city.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-B72-40-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-Brodovitch,_Alexey_p3-3)

At the start of World War I at the young age of 16, Brodovitch abandoned his dream of entering the Imperial Art Academy and ran away from home to join the Russian army. Not long after, his father had him brought home and hired a private tutor to help Alexey finish school. Upon graduating, Brodovitch ran away again on several occasions.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-p12-1) He recalls:
> After a week or so I ran away to the front line to kill Germans. During the Russian Civil War, Brodovitch served with the White Army. While fighting against the Bolsheviks in Odessa, he was badly wounded and was hospitalized for a time in Kislovodsk, in the Caucasus. In 1918, the town was surrounded by the Bolsheviks, forcing Brodovitch into exile. It was during this retreat to the south through Caucasus and Turkey that he met his future wife, Nina.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-B72-40-2)
By good fortune, Alexey's brother Nicolas turned out to be one of the soldiers guarding the refugees in Novorossiysk. Not long after, their father, who had been imprisoned in Saint Petersburg by the Bolsheviks, managed to flee to Novorossiysk in hopes of finding his family. The three were once again together, and arranged for Brodovitch's mother and other relations to join them in Constantinople. Finally reunited, the Brodovitchs made their way to France.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexey_Brodovitch#cite_note-5)

[edit]
Upon arriving in Paris, Brodovitch wanted to be a painter. A Russian white émigré in Paris, Brodovitch found himself poor and having to work for the first time in his life. ## Biography
Alexey Vyacheslavovich Brodovitch was born in 1898 in Ogolichi, then part of the Russian Empire. He served in the Imperial Russian Army during the First World War and the subsequent civil war, fought on the White side, and eventually made his way out of Russia via Constantinople to Paris.
In Paris through the 1920s he moved through the graphic arts — painting sets for the Ballets Russes, designing posters, and winning a poster competition for the Bal Banal in 1924 in which Picasso also entered. He ran the studio at the Parisian department store Trois Quartiers and absorbed the European avant-garde around him — Cassandre’s posters, the Bauhaus émigrés, the Constructivists he already knew from home.
In 1930 he moved to Philadelphia to run the advertising-design programme at the Pennsylvania Museum School of Industrial Art. In 1934 Carmel Snow hired him as art director of _Harper’s Bazaar_. He held the post until 1958 — twenty-four years that remade American magazine design.
From 1941 he ran the Design Laboratory, first at the New School for Social Research and then independently. It was never a conventional course. Students brought work; Brodovitch tore it up. Those who survived included Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Diane Arbus, Hiro and Art Kane.
His later years were difficult. Ill health, alcoholism and two studio fires that destroyed most of his personal archive pushed him into retreat. He returned to France in the mid-1960s and died in Le Thor in 1971, largely in obscurity.

## Design philosophy
Brodovitch’s position was that the editorial spread — not the single page — is the unit of design, and that typography and photography have to be composed as a single image.
> “Astonish me!” — Alexey Brodovitch, to students and contributors
The two-word brief became legendary because it was genuine. He refused to tell photographers what he wanted. He expected them to bring him something he hadn’t seen before, and he edited ruthlessly when they didn’t.
His working principle was that **white space is the designer’s best friend**. A Brodovitch spread is never full. Type sits against deliberately empty paper. An image bleeds across the gutter so that the fold itself becomes part of the composition. Type is treated photographically — its weight and placement answering the weight and placement of the image across the spread.
He was not a theorist. He left no textbook, no manifesto, almost no writing. What he left was the practice and the students who carried it.

## Key works
**Harper’s Bazaar art direction (1934–1958)** — the role that built the reputation. Twenty-four years of monthly issues under Carmel Snow, with Brodovitch commissioning and editing Cartier-Bresson, Man Ray, Bill Brandt, Avedon, Penn and dozens more. The integrated spread — photograph, headline and body treated as one composition — is his permanent contribution to editorial craft.
**Ballet (1945)** — Brodovitch’s own photo book, printed in photogravure in a small edition by J. J. Augustin. Motion-blurred, grainy, deliberately imperfect images of the Ballets Russes taken from the wings during the 1930s. Ignored on publication, now recognised as one of the foundational photo books of the century.
**Portfolio magazine (1949–1951)** — three issues only, co-founded with Frank Zachary. Large format, no advertising, high-quality printing with fold-outs, die-cuts and tipped-in materials. The magazine went bankrupt but every subsequent art-publication designer has studied it.
**Observations (1959)** — book with photographs by Richard Avedon and text by Truman Capote, designed by Brodovitch. The spread discipline from _Bazaar_ applied to the book page — images scaled, cropped and paired against type with complete confidence.
**The Design Laboratory (1941–1967)** — not a physical artefact but a teaching programme. The list of its students is effectively a list of mid-century American photography and design. It may be the longest-lasting work he did.
**WWII Four Freedoms posters (1942)** — a series of Spanish-language propaganda posters for the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. Distributed across Latin America, they show the same cropped-figure composition against open space that Brodovitch used in the magazine context, transferred to the poster format without modification.
**New Poster exhibition catalogue (1937)** — catalogue design for the International Exposition of Design in Outdoor Advertising at the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia. The cover, held at the Library of Congress, shows Brodovitch operating simultaneously as magazine art director, design educator and exhibition designer.

## Key works
### Harper's Bazaar art direction
1934/1958
Twenty-four years as art director of Harper's Bazaar under editor Carmel Snow, from 1934 to 1958. Brodovitch commissioned work from Henri Cartier-Bresson, Man Ray, Bill Brandt, Richard Avedon and Irving Penn, treating each spread as a single composed image rather than a container for separate elements. Issues from this period are held in research collections at institutions including MoMA and the Cooper Hewitt Smithsonian Design Museum in New York.
